{{Short description|Stochastic Markov process}}
{{Orphan|date=October 2025}}

A '''Brownian snake''' is a [[Markov process|stochastic Markov process]] on the space of stopped paths. It has been extensively studied.,<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last=Li |first=Zenghu |chapter=Measure-Valued Branching Processes |date=2011 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-15004-3_2 |title=Measure-Valued Branching Markov Processes |series=Probability and Its Applications |pages=29–56 |editor-last=Li |editor-first=Zenghu |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-15004-3_2 |isbn=978-3-642-15004-3 |access-date=2022-12-20|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Le Gall |first=Jean-Francois |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vfpLfoUQpg8C&dq=le+gall+brownian+snake&pg=PP9 |title=Spatial Branching Processes, Random Snakes and Partial Differential Equations |date=1999-07-01 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-7643-6126-6 |language=en}}</ref> and was in particular successfully used as a representation of [[superprocess]]es.

Informally, superprocesses are the scaling limit of [[branching process]]es, except each particle splits and dies at infinite rates. The Brownian snake is a stochastic object that enables the representation of the genealogy of a superprocess, providing a link between [[Superprocess|super-Brownian motion]] and [[Brownian tree]]s. In other words, even though infinitely many particles are constantly born, we can still keep track of individual trajectories in space, or of when two given present-day particles have split from a common ancestor in the past.

== History ==
The Brownian snake approach was originally developed by [[Jean-François Le Gall]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Le Gall |first=Jean-Francois |date=1991 |title=Brownian Excursions, Trees and Measure-Valued Branching Processes |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2244522 |journal=The Annals of Probability |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=1399–1439 |jstor=2244522 |issn=0091-1798}}</ref> It has since been applied in fragmentation theory,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Abraham |first1=Romain |last2=Serlet |first2=Laurent |date=2002-07-01 |title=Poisson Snake and Fragmentation |journal=Electronic Journal of Probability |volume=7 |issue=none |doi=10.1214/EJP.v7-116 |s2cid=12003800 |issn=1083-6489|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[partial differential equation]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Abraham |first=Romain |date=2000-10-01 |title=Reflecting Brownian snake and a Neumann–Dirichlet problem |journal=Stochastic Processes and Their Applications |language=en |volume=89 |issue=2 |pages=239–260 |doi=10.1016/S0304-4149(00)00027-2 |issn=0304-4149|doi-access=free }}</ref> or [[planar map]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Le Gall |first=Jean-François |date=2019-09-01 |title=Brownian geometry |journal=Japanese Journal of Mathematics |language=en |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=135–174 |doi=10.1007/s11537-019-1821-7 |s2cid=255314865 |issn=1861-3624|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Miermont |first=Grégory |date=2013 |title=The Brownian map is the scaling limit of uniform random plane quadrangulations |journal=Acta Mathematica |volume=210 |issue=2 |pages=319–401 |doi=10.1007/s11511-013-0096-8 |s2cid=119140342 |issn=0001-5962|doi-access=free |arxiv=1104.1606 }}</ref>

== The simplest setting ==
Let <math>D(\R_+,\R)</math> be the space of [[càdlàg]] functions from <math>\R_+</math> to <math>\R</math>, equipped with a metric <math>d</math> compatible with the [[Skorokhod topology]]. We define a '''stopped path''' as a couple <math>(w,z)</math> where <math>w\in D(\R_+,\R)</math> and <math>z\in \R_+</math> are such that <math>w(t)=w(t\wedge z)</math>. In other words, <math>w</math> is constant after <math>z</math>.

Now, we consider a [[jump process]] <math>(J_s^N)_{s\geq 0}</math> with states <math>\{+1,-1\}</math> and jump rate <math>N</math>, such that <math>J^N_0 = +1 </math>. We set:<math display="block">\hat{\beta}^N_s := \int_0^s J^N_{s'}ds'</math>and then <math>\beta^N_s := |\hat{\beta}_s^N|</math> to be the process ''reflected on 0.''

In words, <math>\beta^N_s</math> increases with speed 1, until <math>J^N_s</math> jumps, in which case it decreases with speed 1, and so on. We define the [[stopping time]] <math>\sigma_N</math> to be the <math>N</math>-th hitting time of 0 by <math>\beta^N</math>.
We now define a stochastic process <math>(\eta^N_s,\beta^N_s)_{s\in \R_+}</math> on the set of stopped paths as follows:

* <math>\eta_0^N = 0</math>
* if <math>J^N_s = +1</math> for <math>s\in [s_1,s_2]</math> then:
** <math>\eta_{s_1}(t)=\eta_{s_2}(t)</math> for <math>t\leq \beta_{s_1} </math>
** <math>\Big(\eta_{s_2}(t-\beta_{s_1})-\eta_{s_1}(\beta_{s_1})\Big)_{0\leq t\leq \beta_{s_2}-\beta_{s_1}} </math> is distributed as a Brownian motion independent from <math>\eta_{s_1}</math>
* if <math>J_s^N = -1</math> for <math>s\in [s_1,s_2]</math> then <math>\eta_{s_1}(t)=\eta_{s_2}(t)</math> for <math>t\leq \beta_{s_2}</math>

See animation for an illustration. We call this process a '''snake''' and <math>\beta_s^N</math> the '''head of the snake'''. The path is erased when the snake head moves backwards, and is created anew when it moves forward.

[[File:Gif discrete-time snake.gif|thumb|335x335px|The left panel is the "health bar", which goes to 0 as the number of times the snake hits 0 increases. The panel below just shows how the head of the snake moves. The large panel represents the non-constant part of the snake in black, with the head as a red dot.]]}}

=== Duality with a branching Brownian motion ===
We now consider a measure-valued [[branching process]] <math>(X^N_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> starting with <math>N</math> particles, such that each particle dies with rate <math>N</math>, and upon its death gives birth to two offspring with probability <math>1/2</math>.

On the other hand, we may define from our process <math>(\eta_s^N,\beta_s^N)_{0\leq s\leq \sigma^N}</math> a measure-valued random process <math>\hat{X}_t</math> as follows: note that for any <math>t\in \R_+</math>, there will almost surely be finitely many times <math>s_1,s_2,\dots,s_n\in [0,\sigma^N]</math> such that <math>\beta_{s_i}=t</math>. We then set for any [[measurable function]] <math>f</math>:

<math>\hat{X}^N_t(f):= \sum\limits_{i=1}^nf(\eta^N_s(t))</math>

Then <math>X</math> and <math>\hat{X}</math> are equal in distribution.

== The Brownian snake ==
We take the limit of the previous system as <math>N\to \infty</math>. In this setting, the head of the snake keeps jittering. In fact, the process <math>\beta_s^N</math> tends towards a [[reflected Brownian motion]] <math>\beta_s</math>. The definitions are no longer valid for a number of reasons, in particular because <math>\beta_s</math> is almost surely never monotonous on any interval.

However, we may define a probability <math>R_{a,b}((u,y),d(w,z))</math> on stopped paths such that:

* <math>R_{a,b}</math>-almost surely <math>z=b</math> and <math>w(t)=u(t)</math> for <math>0\leq t\leq a</math>
* The law of <math>(w(a+t))_{0\leq t\leq b-a}</math> is the law of a standard Brownian motion.

We may also define <math>\gamma_s^y(da,db)</math> to be the distribution of <math>(\inf_{0\leq r\leq s}\beta_r,\beta_s)</math> if <math>\beta_0=y</math>. Finally, define the [[Markov chain|transition semigroup]] on the set of stopped paths:

<math>Q_s((u,y),d(w,z)) = \int \gamma_s^y(da,db)R_{a,b}((u,y),d(w,z))</math>

A [[stochastic process]] with this semigroup is called a '''Brownian snake'''.

We may again find a duality between this process and a branching process. Here the branching process will be a [[Superprocess|super-Brownian motion]] <math>(X_t)_{t\in \R_+}</math> with branching mechanism <math>\phi(z)=z^2</math>, started on a [[Dirac delta function|Dirac]] in 0.

However, unlike the previous case, we must be more careful in the definition of the process <math>\hat{X}</math>. Indeed, for <math>t\in \R_+</math> we cannot just list the times <math>s_1,s_2,\dots</math> such that <math>\beta_s=t</math>. Instead we use the [[Local time (mathematics)|local time]] <math>l_s(t)</math> associated with <math>\beta_s</math>: we first define the [[stopping time]] <math>\sigma = \inf\{s\geq 0, l_s(0)\geq u\}</math>. Then we define for any measurable <math>f</math>:<math display="block">\hat{X}_t(f):= \int_0^\sigma f(\eta_s(t))dl_s(t)</math> Then, as before, we obtain that <math>X</math> and <math>\hat{X}</math> are equal in distribution. See the animation for the construction of the branching process from the Brownian snake.
{{Hide|Animation for the branching process associated with the Brownian snake|[[File:Construction of a Branching process associated with the Brownian snake.gif|thumb|350x350px|The left panel shows the "health bar" of the snake, which decreases with the local time the head spends on 0. The panel below shows the movement of the snake head according to a Brownian motion reflected on 0. The central panel shows: in red the head of the current snake, in black the current snake, in green the past snakes. The branching superprocess <math>X</math> is obtained once the health bar reaches 0, by taking all of the green paths.]]}}

== Generalisation ==
The previous example can be generalized in many ways:

* We may consider <math>D(\R_+,E)</math> where <math>(E,d)</math> is a complete separable [[metric space]].
* Instead of a Brownian motion, the underlying movement of the snake can be very general class of Markov processes (see [[Superprocess]]).

== Link with genealogy and the Brownian tree ==
The Brownian snake can be seen as a way to represent the genealogy of a superprocess, the same way a [[Galton-Watson tree]] may encode the hidden genealogy of a [[Galton–Watson process]].<ref name=":1" /> Indeed, for two points of the Brownian snake, their common ancestor will be the infimum of the snake's head position between them.

If we take a Brownian snake and construct a [[real tree]] from it, we obtain a [[Brownian tree]].<ref name=":1" />
